report_title: APT39 / Chafer (G0087) Actor Intelligence Pack — Stage-1 CTI Extraction
source: MITRE ATT&CK G0087 (https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0087/); FireEye/Mandiant 'APT39: An Iranian Cyber Espionage Group Focused on Personal Information' (2019, https://www.mandiant.com/resources/blog/apt39-iranian-cyber-espionage-group-focused-on-personal-information); FBI FLASH CU-000151-MW / U.S. Treasury OFAC & DOJ actions on Rana Intelligence Computing (Sept 2020); Symantec 'Chafer' reporting (Dec 2015 / Feb 2018); Bitdefender Chafer reporting; CISA MAR-10297887-1.v2 'Iranian Web Shells' (AR20-259A, https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/analysis-reports/ar20-259a)

actor.name: APT39
related_clusters: Rana Intelligence Computing (OFAC-sanctioned front company, Sept 2020)
Iran Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS)
actor.attribution: Iran-nexus; cyber espionage activity conducted by Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) through the front company Rana Intelligence Computing since at least 2014, per MITRE ATT&CK G0087, FireEye/Mandiant (2019), and the September 2020 U.S. Government actions (FBI FLASH, DOJ indictments, and OFAC sanctions designating Rana Intelligence Computing and named individuals). APT39 focuses on personal-information tracking and surveillance of individuals and entities considered a threat by the MOIS.

key_campaigns.name: APT39 personal-information tracking operations
key_campaigns.summary: Long-running MOIS surveillance operations prioritizing monitoring, tracking, and surveillance of specific individuals. Heavy targeting of telecommunications and travel/tourism sectors (which hold PII, travel records, and location/movement data) to enable tracking of persons of interest across the Middle East and beyond.

key_campaigns.name: Chafer telecom & travel intrusions (Gulf focus)
key_campaigns.summary: Symantec/Bitdefender-tracked Chafer activity against telecommunications and travel companies in the Middle East, using spear-phishing, SQL injection against public-facing servers, web shells (ANTAK, ASPXSpy), and post-exploitation tooling (Mimikatz, custom keyloggers, Remexi backdoor) to harvest credentials and monitor targets.

key_campaigns.name: Rana Intelligence Computing designation
key_campaigns.summary: U.S. Treasury OFAC sanctioned Rana Intelligence Computing Company as a MOIS front for APT39; DOJ unsealed indictments and the FBI released a FLASH (CU-000151-MW) detailing malware and TTPs. Confirmed the MOIS/Rana operational link and the personal-surveillance mission.

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used credential-dumping tools such as Mimikatz, ProcDump, and Windows Credential Editor to steal credentials from compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — execution of Mimikatz/ProcDump/WCE and process access to credential stores is highly observable in EDR and process-access telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used ProcDump and Mimikatz to dump LSASS memory to extract credentials.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — process access to lsass.exe (handle open, ProcDump -ma lsass) and Mimikatz signatures are strong, well-covered detections

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has collected data and files of interest (PII, travel/movement records, documents) from compromised local systems as part of its personal-information tracking mission.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — bulk local file collection is common; suspicious mainly via staging/archiving lineage and access to unusual document stores

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has queried the Windows registry to gather system and configuration information on compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — reg query is common; value comes from watching sensitive keys in a recon-burst/process-lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used tools such as nbtscan and custom scripts to identify remote systems on the victim network prior to lateral movement.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — remote-host enumeration (nbtscan/ping sweeps) is detectable via connection-fanout analytics and known-tool execution signatures

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used RDP with stolen credentials for lateral movement within compromised environments.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — RDP lateral movement is detectable via 4624 type-10 logons, internal-RDP fanout, and impossible-travel analytics; a strong detection surface given APT39's reliance on valid-account RDP

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used PsExec and SMB/admin shares (e.g. ADMIN$, C$) to move laterally and execute payloads on remote hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — SMB admin-share access and PsExec service creation (7045/5145) are strongly detectable in Windows and network telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used SSH (including PLINK) to access and move between compromised systems.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — SSH client execution and outbound SSH from unusual hosts are detectable via process + network telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used packers/crypters to obfuscate malware payloads and hinder static analysis and signature detection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — packed binaries are detectable via entropy/section anomalies and packer signatures but require dedicated static scanning

ttps.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Encrypted/Encoded File
ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has encrypted and encoded payloads and staged data (including base64) to evade detection and inspection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — high-entropy/encoded files are detectable via file-entropy analytics but require dedicated scanning

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has run whoami and similar commands to identify the current user and privilege context on compromised systems.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — whoami is common; value is in process-lineage correlation (spawned by script host / web shell)

ttps.technique_name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has named malware and tools to masquerade as legitimate files/processes and placed them in plausible locations to blend in.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — legit-looking names in non-standard paths are detectable via path/name baselining and signature-vs-name mismatch

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has exfiltrated stolen data (credentials, PII, documents) back to attacker infrastructure over its established command-and-control channels.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — exfil embedded in the C2 channel blends with beacon traffic; hunt on outbound volume anomalies and long-lived sessions

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has scanned victim networks to identify open ports and reachable services prior to lateral movement.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — scanning bursts are detectable via network/connection-fanout analytics and known-tool signatures

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has created scheduled tasks to establish persistence and to execute payloads on compromised systems.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — scheduled-task creation is logged (Event ID 4698 / Task Scheduler operational) and highly detectable, especially with script/executable actions

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has captured user input using keyloggers and related tooling to monitor targeted individuals.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — input-capture APIs leave little discrete log signal; behavioral/EDR hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has deployed custom keyloggers to capture keystrokes and harvest credentials and monitor persons of interest.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — keystroke-hooking leaves little discrete log signal; behavioral/EDR hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used various command and scripting interpreters for execution on compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — generic parent; value comes from specific interpreter sub-techniques with process-lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used PowerShell (including POWBAT/POWERSTATS-adjacent tooling) to execute commands and stage payloads.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — script-block/module logging and suspicious PowerShell parenting are core, well-covered detections

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used Visual Basic scripts and macros in delivery documents to execute payloads.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — wscript/cscript executing VBS, especially spawned by Office, is a strong detectable signal

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used Python-based tooling/scripts for execution on compromised systems.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — python.exe execution in enterprise contexts is detectable via process telemetry and unusual interpreter presence on non-dev hosts

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: AutoHotKey & AutoIT
ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used AutoIt-based scripting for execution and to automate malicious tasks.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — AutoIt/AutoHotKey interpreter execution is detectable via process telemetry and is unusual in most enterprise baselines

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has deleted tools, logs, and payload files after use to remove forensic artifacts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — file deletion is detectable via file-system audit / EDR delete events but is noisy and needs correlation with prior payload writes

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used HTTP/HTTPS-based C2 for its backdoors (e.g. Remexi and web-shell interaction).
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — HTTP(S) C2 is detectable via proxy/beacon analytics and URI/JA3 anomalies but blends with normal web traffic

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used DNS as a command-and-control channel for certain tooling.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — DNS-based C2 is detectable via query-length/entropy/volume analytics and NXDOMAIN patterns, but requires full DNS logging that is frequently under-instrumented

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has staged collected data locally (often archived) prior to exfiltration.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — local staging is common; suspicious when tied to archiving utilities writing large archives to temp/staging paths

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used stolen/valid credentials to access systems and remote services (RDP, VPN, OWA), blending in with legitimate activity — a core APT39 access and persistence pattern.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — valid-account abuse is detectable via anomalous logon analytics (impossible travel, new host/time, first-seen device) but blends with legitimate use; a strong identity-monitoring detection surface for APT39

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has enumerated files and directories to locate data of interest and stage collection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — file/directory enumeration is ubiquitous; better as a hunt in tight recon-burst lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used internal proxies/relays to route C2 traffic between compromised hosts inside victim networks.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — internal proxy relays are subtle; hunt on unexpected host-to-host relay patterns and internal listeners

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has routed C2 through external proxy infrastructure to obscure the true destination of traffic.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — external proxy chains are off-victim; hunt on connections to known proxy/anonymization endpoints

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used legitimate web services for bidirectional C2 communication to blend with normal traffic.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — legitimate-web-service C2 blends with sanctioned SaaS traffic; hunt on anomalous automation patterns to those services

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has downloaded additional tools and payloads onto compromised systems, including via certutil and BITS.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — remote downloads via certutil/BITS and unexpected inbound file writes are strongly detectable in process + network telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used brute-force and credential-guessing techniques to obtain account credentials.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — brute force is detectable via authentication-failure spikes (4625) and lockout telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used custom tools to capture screenshots of targeted users' desktops as part of surveillance.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — screen-capture APIs leave little discrete log signal; behavioral/EDR hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has collected clipboard data from compromised systems as part of its information-gathering.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — clipboard-capture leaves little discrete log signal; behavioral/EDR hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has enumerated network shares to identify accessible data repositories for collection and lateral movement.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — 'net view' / share enumeration is detectable via command-line logging in recon-burst context

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has created local accounts on compromised systems to maintain persistent access.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — local account creation is logged (Event ID 4720) and is a high-fidelity persistence detection

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has decoded/deobfuscated payloads and staged data at runtime (including base64 decoding via certutil/scripts).
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — 'certutil -decode' and script-based decode routines are directly observable in command-line and script-block logging

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 (Chafer) has used SQL injection against public-facing web/database servers as an initial-access vector, frequently followed by web-shell deployment.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — SQLi and public-app exploitation are detectable via WAF/web-server logs and anomalous DB-to-webserver process behavior; the SQLi-to-webshell chain is a signature APT39 pattern warranting targeted web-tier monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has used Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) jobs to download/transfer files while evading detection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — BITS jobs are detectable via BITS-Client operational logs and bitsadmin/PowerShell BITS cmdlet command-lines, but require targeted logging

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has relied on targets clicking malicious links delivered via spear-phishing to achieve execution.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — malicious-link clicks are detectable via email/URL-gateway and proxy logs; endpoint signal is indirect

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has relied on targets opening malicious attachments (often macro-enabled documents) to execute payloads.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — Office apps spawning script/child processes after macro enablement is a core detectable behavior

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has deployed web shells (ANTAK and ASPXSpy) on Internet-facing IIS/web servers, often following SQL injection, to maintain persistent remote access and execute commands.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — web shells are detectable via web-server worker processes (w3wp.exe) spawning cmd/powershell, new/modified .aspx files in web roots, and anomalous IIS request patterns; ANTAK/ASPXSpy web-shell use is a signature APT39 tradecraft and a prime detection surface

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has abused the AppInit_DLLs registry mechanism to load malicious DLLs for persistence.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — modification of HKLM\...\Windows\AppInit_DLLs is a rare, high-fidelity registry-modification detection

ttps.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has established persistence via Registry Run keys and Startup-folder entries to auto-execute malware at logon.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — Run-key writes and Startup-folder drops are detectable via registry-modification and file-creation telemetry (Autoruns-class monitoring)

ttps.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Shortcut Modification
ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has modified/created shortcut (.lnk) files to establish persistence and trigger payload execution.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — malicious .lnk creation/modification in startup/user paths is detectable via file-creation telemetry and shortcut-target analysis

ttps.technique_name: Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing Policy Modification
ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has modified code-signing/driver-signature enforcement policy to allow unsigned or attacker-controlled code to load.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — signing-policy/DSE modifications (bcdedit testsigning, registry policy changes) are detectable via command-line and registry telemetry but require targeted rules

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has harvested stored credentials from password stores on compromised systems.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — credential-store access is detectable mainly via known-tool execution signatures and file/vault access telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility
ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has archived collected data with utilities (e.g. WinRAR) prior to exfiltration.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — archiving-utility execution producing large archives in staging paths is detectable via process + file-creation telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has sent spear-phishing emails with malicious attachments (often macro documents) to targeted individuals for initial access.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — attachment-based spearphishing is detectable via mail sandboxing and macro-content analysis at the gateway

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has sent spear-phishing emails with malicious links to credential-harvesting or malware-delivery pages.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — link-based spearphishing is detectable via URL rewriting/detonation and proxy telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has executed payloads by creating/starting Windows services (including via PsExec) on local and remote hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — service creation/execution (Event ID 7045 / 4697) is strongly detectable, especially with anomalous binary paths

ttps.procedure_description: APT39 has obtained and used publicly available tools including Mimikatz, ProcDump, Windows Credential Editor, PsExec, and PLINK.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — tool acquisition itself is off-endpoint; downstream use is where detection lands — this entry is a hunt/intel candidate

detection_signals: IIS/web-server worker process (w3wp.exe) spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe, and new/modified .aspx files in web roots (ANTAK / ASPXSpy web shells)
SQL injection patterns in web/DB server logs followed by web-shell file writes (APT39 SQLi-to-webshell initial-access chain)
ProcDump '-ma lsass' / Mimikatz / Windows Credential Editor execution or handle-open access to lsass.exe
PsExec service creation (Event ID 7045) and SMB admin-share access (5145) for lateral movement
RDP type-10 (Event ID 4624) logons from unusual internal hosts using recently compromised valid accounts
Local account creation (Event ID 4720) not tied to IT provisioning (persistence)
Registry Run-key writes, Startup-folder drops, AppInit_DLLs modification, and malicious .lnk creation (persistence)
certutil '-decode' / '-urlcache' and bitsadmin/BITS-Client operational events transferring payloads
Scheduled-task creation (Event ID 4698) invoking script hosts or attacker binaries
AutoIt / python.exe interpreter execution on hosts with no legitimate baseline for them
Anomalous valid-account authentication (impossible travel, new device/time) — APT39 relies heavily on stolen credentials and remote services (RDP/VPN/OWA)
Archiving utilities (WinRAR) producing large archives in temp/staging paths prior to outbound transfer (collection/exfil staging)
notes: All 53 MITRE ATT&CK G0087 techniques were verified present in this environment's bundled ATT&CK dataset (sigma.data.mitre_attack) before emission; zero techniques were dropped as invalid. Enrichment IDs were also verified valid but no non-G0087 techniques were added — the extraction stays anchored to the authoritative G0087 group-technique mapping, enriched with APT39/Chafer-specific procedure descriptions, observed tooling, detection_feasibility hints (the field decision-agent routes on), and source citations. Tactic slugs follow the environment convention: the defense-evasion tactic is emitted as 'stealth' (applies to T1027.002, T1027.013, T1036.005, T1070.004, T1078, T1140, T1197, T1553.006). No T1685/T1686 Impair-Defenses-family techniques are in the G0087 base, so the 'defense-impairment' tactic is not used here. Multi-tactic techniques were collapsed to a single primary tactic for routing (e.g. T1053.005->persistence, T1078->stealth, T1546.010->persistence, T1569.002->execution, T1056.001->credential-access). Attribution to Iran/MOIS via the Rana Intelligence Computing front company is HIGH confidence per MITRE G0087, FireEye/Mandiant (2019), and the September 2020 U.S. Government actions (FBI FLASH CU-000151-MW, DOJ indictments, OFAC sanctions). APT39's distinguishing mission is personal-information tracking/surveillance of individuals, with heavy telecom and travel/tourism targeting across the Gulf to obtain PII and movement/location data. Signature detection surfaces flagged in feasibility hints: (1) ANTAK/ASPXSpy web shells on IIS (T1505.003 high), (2) SQLi-to-webshell public-app exploitation (T1190 medium), (3) valid-account + RDP/SMB/PsExec lateral movement (T1078/T1021.001/T1021.002/T1569.002 medium-high), (4) LSASS credential dumping via ProcDump/Mimikatz/WCE (T1003/T1003.001 high). IOCs are deliberately EMPTY: MITRE G0087 lists no concrete IOCs, and the primary APT39/Rana FBI FLASH (CU-000151-MW) was not machine-fetchable in this pass. A CISA Malware Analysis Report was successfully fetched (AR20-259A, MAR-10297887-1.v2 'Iranian Web Shells', 55 SHA256 web-shell samples), but that MAR is attributed to Iranian government cyber actors BROADLY and is associated with the 2020 web-shell/vulnerability-exploitation wave rather than being cleanly attributed to Rana/APT39; per the no-hallucinated-IOC rule and to avoid poisoning downstream attribution, those hashes are NOT asserted here as APT39 indicators. They should be reviewed and, if a per-sample APT39/Rana linkage is established from the FBI FLASH or Mandiant/Symantec appendices, ingested directly from that source. Malware and tooling names (Remexi, Cadelspy, ANTAK, ASPXSpy, POWBAT, Mimikatz, ProcDump, WCE, PsExec, PLINK) are well-established public attributions and are listed under malware[]/tooling_observed[] rather than as raw IOCs. Lower-feasibility hunt candidates (vs detection candidates): T1005, T1041, T1083, T1090.001, T1090.002, T1102.002, T1056, T1056.001, T1113, T1115, T1588.002.
